strengths: Addresses a practical and well-motivated problem: closing the performance gap between memory-efficient target-free methods and target-based methods, which is relevant given the trend toward scaling Q-networks.

The proposed method (iS-QN) is simple, elegant, and easy to implement as a modification to DQN/CQL, requiring only a small increase in parameters (extra linear heads) rather than doubling network size.
Extensive empirical evaluation across multiple settings: online and offline RL, two architectures (CNN and IMPALA), with and without LayerNorm, and both DQN and CQL, showing consistent trends.
Good use of rigorous statistical practices (IQM, stratified bootstrap CIs, AUC as primary metric) following Agarwal et al. 2021 recommendations.

Provides mechanistic insight into why the method works via gradient cosine similarity analysis and effective rank (srank) of representations, which helps explain rather than just demonstrate the improvement.
The ablation with Ensemble Shared Features (ES-CQL) supports the generality of the 'shared linear head' idea beyond the iterated Q-learning framing.
The paper is well-written and clearly positioned relative to a large body of related work on target-network alternatives and regularization techniques.
weaknesses: Evaluation is restricted to discrete-action Atari (DQN/CQL); no continuous-control experiments are included despite the method's clear motivation for large actor-critic networks (e.g., CrossQ-like settings) — the authors even mention continuous action spaces as future work, leaving a significant application area for target-free methods untested.

The number of Atari games is fairly small (15, further reduced to 10 for IMPALA and offline experiments) for AUC-based conclusions, and choice of K (number of heads) appears to require environment/architecture-specific tuning (K=49 hurts for CNN but helps for IMPALA), suggesting sensitivity that isn't fully characterized.

No wall-clock/compute overhead analysis is given beyond a qualitative claim of 'comparable training time'; given the loss sums over K Bellman terms and stores K+1 heads, some quantitative compute comparison would strengthen the memory-vs-compute tradeoff argument.

The head architecture only replaces the last linear layer; it's unclear how sensitive results are to using more than one shared layer as target vs. only the head, i.e. there's limited ablation on how much of the network should be shared versus separate.

Some claims (e.g., 'iS-DQN K=9 outperforms target-based approach by 6%') are based on a single run of AUC comparison with fairly wide/overlapping confidence intervals in places (e.g., Figure 3 left, K=49 box overlaps with TB-DQN), and statistical significance of the improvement over TB is not clearly established.

The paper does not compare against other lightweight alternatives to a full target network (e.g., Polyak averaging with different rates, EMA of only certain layers) which could serve as simpler baselines achieving similar memory savings.

The related regularization techniques (e.g., CrossQ/BatchNorm) are shown to underperform in the discrete setting but this is based on limited games (Figure 12 right, only 5 games), which weakens the strength of this comparison.

strengths: Addresses a practically relevant tension (memory footprint of target networks vs. capacity of online network) with a simple, elegant architectural idea: sharing all but the last linear layer between online and target networks.

Combines this with the existing iterated Q-learning concept in a sensible way (iS-QN), turning a 2K-network method into a single network with K+1 lightweight heads, which is a reasonable engineering contribution.

Reasonably rigorous evaluation protocol: IQM with stratified bootstrap confidence intervals (Agarwal et al., 2021), normalized AUC to track sample efficiency, and both online (DQN) and offline (CQL) settings.

Includes diagnostic analyses (gradient cosine similarity to target-based updates, effective rank/srank of representations, dormant neuron counts) that provide some mechanistic insight into why the method helps, beyond pure performance numbers.
Additional ablation (Ensemble Shared Features) shows the core idea of parameter sharing is not limited to the iterated Q-learning instantiation, suggesting some generality.
Reports both positive and negative results honestly (e.g., K=49 sometimes hurting with CNN, BatchNorm hurting in discrete control), which adds credibility.
weaknesses: Despite the introduction and related work heavily motivating the need for target-free methods in continuous-control / actor-critic settings (CrossQ, streaming RL, high-dimensional/multi-modal applications), all experiments are restricted to discrete-action Atari with DQN/CQL; no continuous-control validation is provided, leaving the central motivating use case untested.

Evaluation is conducted on small Atari subsets (15 games, reduced to 10 for IMPALA experiments) rather than the standard 57-game suite, which limits confidence in generalization of the AUC/IQM conclusions.

The number of heads K is an important new hyperparameter whose optimal value is architecture- and setting-dependent (e.g., K=49 helps for IMPALA but hurts for CNN) without a principled method or guidance for selecting it a priori, undermining practical applicability.

Confidence intervals in several key figures (e.g., comparing K=9 vs K=49, or dormant neuron comparisons) appear to overlap, raising doubts about the statistical robustness of some of the paper's specific claims (e.g., iS-DQN K=9 'outperforming' TB-DQN by 6%).
The abstract/claims of 'comparable training time' to target-based methods are not substantiated with explicit wall-clock or compute benchmarking tables in the main text.
No code is released at submission time ('will be made open source'), limiting reproducibility assessment during review.

The mechanistic explanations (cosine similarity, effective rank) are correlational observations rather than a theoretical analysis of why/when the shared-feature + iterated-head construction should match or exceed target-based stability, leaving the core phenomenon not fully explained.

The method still requires roughly 50% of the online network's extra parameters (compared to true target-free), so it is a compromise rather than a full solution to the memory problem motivating the paper; the practical benefit over simply using a slightly larger target-free network is not directly compared.

strengths: The core idea is simple, well-motivated, and elegant: representing the target network as a frozen copy of only the last linear layer while sharing the feature extractor with the online network, which naturally generalizes to multiple heads for iterated Bellman updates.

Extensive empirical evaluation across multiple settings: online and offline RL, two different architectures (CNN, IMPALA), with and without LayerNorm, and multiple values of K, providing a fairly comprehensive picture of the method's behavior.

Good experimental rigor: use of IQM with stratified bootstrap confidence intervals, 5 seeds per game, normalized AUC as the primary sample-efficiency metric, and per-game learning curves reported in the appendix.

Insightful analysis attempting to explain *why* the method works, via gradient cosine similarity with the target-based approach and effective rank (srank) of learned representations, going beyond simple performance numbers.

Demonstrates a favorable memory/performance trade-off, e.g., iS-DQN K=9 matches or exceeds target-based performance while using roughly half the parameters, which is a practically meaningful contribution given the motivation of scaling network capacity under memory constraints.

Shows generality of the underlying idea (parameter/feature sharing) beyond iterated Q-learning through the Ensemble Shared Features (ES-CQL) variant, and demonstrates orthogonality to other techniques like LayerNorm.
Clear, well-organized presentation with helpful conceptual figures (Fig. 1, 2) situating the method relative to target-based/target-free baselines.
weaknesses: The evaluation is restricted entirely to discrete-action Atari-style benchmarks (DQN/CQL); continuous control, which is explicitly mentioned as a motivating application area in the introduction (e.g., robotics, high-dimensional state spaces), is left entirely to future work, limiting the generality of the claims implied by the title.

Only two base algorithms (DQN and CQL) are tested; no comparison to more modern/stronger target-free stabilization baselines (e.g., DeepMellow, CrossQ-style methods, gradient TD methods) is performed empirically within the same experimental pipeline, despite being discussed in related work.

Due to computational budget constraints, only 15 (and 10 for IMPALA) Atari games are used, which is a relatively small and potentially non-representative subset, raising some concern about the robustness/generalizability of the reported gains.

The mechanistic explanation for why iS-QN helps is largely empirical/correlational (gradient cosine similarity, srank) rather than grounded in theoretical analysis or convergence guarantees, despite prior work (Schmitt et al. 2022) providing such guarantees for related ideas in the linear case.

Sensitivity of the method to its own hyperparameters (target update period T, the window-shift period D from i-QN, choice of K) is not systematically ablated beyond varying K, leaving open questions about robustness and tuning effort in new settings.

The decline in performance at very large K (e.g., K=49 for the CNN architecture) is only conjectured to stem from limited representation capacity, without further empirical verification (e.g., increasing network width to test the hypothesis).

Baseline hyperparameters are kept at standard DQN values without retuning for the modified architecture, which could understate the achievable performance of target-based/target-free baselines and slightly bias comparisons in favor of the proposed method.

strengths: The core idea is simple, elegant, and cheap to implement: sharing feature parameters between online and target networks while keeping only a frozen linear head as the 'target', combined with iterated Q-learning heads, is a clever way to reduce memory footprint while retaining stability benefits of target networks.

Extensive empirical evaluation across a diverse set of settings: online Atari (CNN and IMPALA architectures), offline Atari (CQL), continuous control (DMC Hard with SimbaV2/SAC), and even large-scale language RL (ILQL on Wordle with GPT-2), which is a broad and convincing testbed for a resource-efficiency claim.

Good use of statistically rigorous evaluation practices (IQM, stratified bootstrap CIs, AUC normalization) following Agarwal et al. (2021) recommendations, and reporting per-game learning curves in the appendix for transparency.

Ablations and analyses (Section 5.5) attempting to explain why the method works—gradient cosine similarity to target-based updates, target churn, and effective rank/srank analysis—add some mechanistic insight beyond pure benchmarking.
The paper reports both memory savings (parameter counts) and confirms no substantial increase in training time/FLOPs (Appendix B), directly supporting the practical resource-efficiency motivation.
The related work section is thorough and clearly positions the contribution relative to prior target-free methods, regularization techniques, and iterated Q-learning literature.
The additional Ensemble Shared Features (ES-CQL) variant shows the parameter-sharing idea generalizes beyond the specific iterated-Q-learning instantiation, strengthening the generality claim.
weaknesses: The number of heads K is an important new hyperparameter whose optimal value varies unpredictably across settings and architectures (e.g., K=9 best for CNN, K=49 better for IMPALA, K=1~K=9 similar for SAC), and no clear principled guidance or automatic selection method is given, which limits practical usability and adds tuning burden that partially offsets the claimed simplicity/efficiency advantage.

The theoretical justification is fairly thin: the paper leans heavily on empirical demonstration and post-hoc explanatory diagnostics (cosine similarity, target churn, srank) without a formal analysis of convergence or stability guarantees for the shared-feature target construction, unlike some cited prior works (e.g., Schmitt et al., 2022) that provide theoretical guarantees for related ideas.

Baseline hyperparameters are explicitly not retuned for the new architectures/algorithms ('the same hyperparameters as those provided in the original target-based approaches are used without further tuning'), which raises concern that comparisons might be somewhat unfair or that the target-free/iS-QN variants could be further improved (or the target-based baseline underperforming) with proper tuning specific to each method.

Some datasets/domains use relatively few seeds or limited numbers of tasks/games (5 seeds per Atari game with 15 or 10 games, 7 DMC tasks), and although CIs are reported, the effect sizes in several comparisons (e.g., iS-SAC K=1 vs K=9 overlapping with TB-SAC) are sometimes marginal, making some specific numerical claims (e.g., '6% improvement over target-based') less robust than presented.

The mechanism claims in Section 5.5 (e.g., 'target churn', gradient cosine similarity) are somewhat ad hoc metrics introduced specifically for this paper without independent validation or comparison to established diagnostic tools, and the causal story linking these metrics to final performance is more suggestive/correlational than rigorously established.

The paper's headline claim of 'bridging the performance gap' and sometimes 'outperforming' target-based methods (e.g., iS-DQN K=9 beating TB-DQN by 6%) could be partly attributable to the additional loss terms/heads acting as an implicit auxiliary/regularization signal rather than purely to the shared-feature trick; the paper does not fully disentangle the contribution of iterated Q-learning's auxiliary heads from the shared-feature mechanism in a controlled way (e.g., an ablation with separate non-shared iterated heads at equal head count is not clearly presented as a controlled comparison in the main text).

The paper does not report wall-clock or memory comparisons against alternative resource-efficient methods (e.g., pruning, quantization, or other streaming-only baselines like Vasan et al. 2024, Gallici et al. 2025) which are mentioned in related work but not empirically benchmarked, limiting the completeness of the 'resource-efficient RL' positioning.

Loss aggregation design choice (summing K Bellman losses) is acknowledged as ad hoc and left for future work, and the one alternative explored (discounting future terms in SAC) is applied inconsistently across experiments, suggesting the method's default recipe may not be robust/well-optimized across settings.

strengths: The core idea—sharing the feature extractor between online and target networks while only maintaining a separate copy of the final linear head(s)—is simple, intuitive, and provides a clear, practical mechanism to reduce memory footprint without fully sacrificing stabilization benefits of target networks.

Combining the shared-feature idea with iterated Q-learning (multiple linear heads approximating consecutive Bellman iterations) is a natural and reasonably novel extension that leverages an existing technique (i-QN) in a new resource-efficient way.

The empirical evaluation spans a wide variety of settings: online/offline discrete control (Atari with CNN and IMPALA architectures), continuous control (DMC Hard with SimbaV2/SAC), and a language-model-based offline RL task (Wordle with GPT-2), which is a relatively broad and ambitious evaluation suite for a single paper.

Useful diagnostic analyses are provided (gradient cosine similarity, target churn, effective rank/srank, dormant neurons) that attempt to explain why the method works, going beyond pure performance numbers.
Memory savings are concretely quantified (e.g., 49% parameter reduction in SAC/DMC, 33% RAM savings in the language task), which supports the paper's stated motivation of resource efficiency.

The method is orthogonal to existing regularization approaches (LayerNorm, BatchNorm) and the paper demonstrates it can be combined with these, as well as being applicable beyond DQN (to CQL, SAC, ILQL), suggesting some generality.
weaknesses: The number of heads K is a new hyperparameter with inconsistent optimal values across settings (K=9 best for CNN Atari, K=49 better for IMPALA, K=1 roughly as good as K=9 for SAC/DMC), and the paper offers no principled way to select K other than post-hoc trial and error, undermining the claimed practicality of the method.

The memory savings claims are somewhat overstated/narrow: the paper itself shows in Figure 10 that training time and FLOPs are essentially unchanged relative to target-based methods in most settings, meaning the main benefit is restricted to parameter/VRAM storage, not compute — this should be more prominently caveated in the abstract/intro rather than buried in limitations.

Many of the Atari evaluations use only 15 (or 10) games out of the standard 57, and only 5 seeds, which is a relatively small and potentially cherry-picked subset (chosen for 'diversity of normalized return' by the authors), raising concerns about statistical robustness and generalizability of the AUC/IQM comparisons, especially given confidence intervals in several figures (e.g., Fig 3, 4) are fairly wide and overlapping between methods.

The core theoretical contribution is incremental: iS-QN is essentially a straightforward combination of two existing ideas (iterated Q-learning from Vincent et al. 2025, and the well-known concept of shared-trunk/multi-head Q-networks already used in DQN's own output head design) — the paper does not provide new theoretical guarantees (e.g., convergence) for the shared-feature variant, unlike the original i-QN paper which proved convergence for linear function approximation.

The explanation for why iS-QN works (Section 5.5) is largely post-hoc and correlational (gradient cosine similarity, target churn, srank) rather than a rigorous causal or theoretical account; these metrics are suggestive but do not establish why sharing features specifically produces the observed stabilizing effect, especially given that in several ablations the benefit plateaus or reverses at high K (K=49 Atari CNN) without a clear predictive theory.

Hyperparameters are explicitly stated to be inherited from original target-based baselines without retuning for the target-free/iS-QN variants, which could bias comparisons against the proposed method or alternatively mean the comparison is not fully optimized for any approach, weakening the fairness/strength of the comparative claims.

The paper's writing can be dense and the real takeaway (when to use which K, what trade-offs emerge, and how to pick K a priori for a new task) is not clearly synthesized, leaving practitioners without clear actionable guidance despite the stated motivation of resource efficiency for real-world/edge applications.

The Wordle/language experiment, while interesting, is relatively small-scale (GPT-2 small, single benchmark) and does not strongly establish scaling behavior to larger, more realistic LLM-RL settings that the introduction's motivation (mixtures of experts, multi-modal inputs, etc.) implies should matter most.

Some ablation choices seem somewhat ad hoc, e.g., scaling future loss terms by 0.25 for SAC without deeper justification, and the paper explicitly defers investigation of alternative loss aggregation schemes to future work, suggesting the current design may not be fully optimized or robust.

strengths: Simple, well-motivated idea: sharing the feature extractor between online and target networks and only duplicating the last linear layer, substantially reducing the memory footprint compared to full target networks while retaining most of the benefits of target-based learning.

Very broad and diverse empirical evaluation spanning online discrete control (Atari, two architectures), offline discrete control (CQL on Atari), continuous control (SAC with SimbaV2 on DMC Hard), and even a language-model RL setting (ILQL with GPT-2 on Wordle), which convincingly demonstrates the generality of the approach.
Rigorous statistical reporting following best practices (IQM, stratified bootstrap CIs, AUC normalized by target-based baseline), which strengthens the credibility of the comparisons.

Thoughtful mechanistic analysis (gradient cosine similarity to target-based updates, a newly introduced 'target churn' metric, and effective rank/srank of representations) that provides plausible explanations for why the shared-feature/iterated approach narrows the target-free vs target-based gap.
Additional variant (Ensemble Shared Features) shows the core idea of sharing parameters generalizes beyond the specific iterated Q-learning instantiation, strengthening the generality claim.

Transparent reporting of limitations, including cases where the method underperforms (e.g., large K degrading performance on the CNN architecture, no reduction in training time/FLOPs), and honest treatment of interactions with normalization layers.
Strong reproducibility effort: code is shared, hyperparameters are extensively documented in the appendix, and individual per-game learning curves are provided.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution (freezing/sharing all but the last layer as a 'target') is a relatively simple architectural trick; the paper itself notes this is conceptually similar to existing multi-head DQN designs, which somewhat limits the novelty relative to prior target-free/regularization literature.

The method introduces K as a new hyperparameter whose optimal value appears highly setting-dependent (differs across CNN vs IMPALA vs continuous control), and no principled method for selecting K a priori is provided beyond empirical sweeps.

No theoretical convergence analysis or formal guarantees are given for iS-QN; all support is empirical/qualitative (gradient similarity, churn, srank), which is suggestive but not conclusive as to why the method works.
As explicitly acknowledged, the approach only reduces memory, not compute/training time or FLOPs (except in the ILQL case), somewhat narrowing the claimed 'resource efficiency' contribution.

The use of normalization layers (LayerNorm/BatchNorm) is applied inconsistently across baselines within a domain (e.g., BatchNorm excluded for TB-SAC and TB-DQN because it hurts them), which, while justified, could still raise questions about the fairness/comprehensiveness of some comparisons.

Experimental scope per domain remains moderate (15/10 Atari games, 7 DMC tasks, a single language task), typical for RL papers but still limiting the strength of generality claims across the full space of RL problems.

Limited comparison against other existing memory-efficient or target-free baselines beyond vanilla target-free/target-based versions (e.g., other regularization-based target-free methods are discussed but not directly benchmarked against iS-QN in the main experiments).

strengths: Introduces a simple and practical idea (sharing feature parameters between online and target networks, represented via linear heads) that meaningfully reduces the target-free vs target-based performance gap while keeping a low memory footprint.
Combines the shared-features idea with iterated Q-learning in a natural way (iS-QN), and shows this combination provides further gains beyond simply sharing features (K=1).

Extremely broad empirical validation: online discrete control (Atari, two architectures, with/without normalization), offline discrete control (CQL), continuous control (SAC/SimbaV2), language-model-based offline RL (ILQL/Wordle), and streaming RL (Stream Q(λ)) — demonstrating generality of the approach across very different algorithmic and architectural settings.

Includes thoughtful analysis of the underlying mechanism: gradient cosine similarity to target-based updates, a novel 'target churn' metric, and effective rank (srank) of representations, providing some mechanistic insight into why the method works.

Extensive ablations (target update period T, number of heads K, network width, meta-learned per-head loss weighting) and additional experiments (MellowMax combination, mixed-precision training) that stress-test robustness and generality of the method.

Good reproducibility practices: detailed hyperparameter tables, per-game learning curves in the appendix, code availability implied, and transparent reporting of training time/FLOPs showing the memory savings do not come from reduced compute.

Orthogonality to existing target-free regularization techniques (MellowMax, BatchNorm/LayerNorm) is explicitly demonstrated, showing the method can be layered on top of prior work rather than being mutually exclusive with it.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is somewhat incremental: it largely stitches together two existing ideas (a shared-backbone target head and iterated Q-learning from Vincent et al. 2025b) rather than introducing a fundamentally new mechanism.

The number of Bellman iterations K is an important new hyperparameter with no principled selection rule; the paper only offers a heuristic 'increase until it stops helping,' and the optimal K varies considerably across domains/architectures (e.g., K=49 helps for IMPALA but hurts for CNN), which complicates practical deployment.

Some result comparisons appear to have overlapping confidence intervals (e.g., iS-SAC K=9 said to be 'on par' with target-based approach in DMC), which slightly weakens the strength of some headline claims of closing the gap.

The reported memory savings do not translate into reduced training time or FLOPs (as the authors themselves acknowledge), limiting the practical benefit to memory-constrained settings only, which somewhat narrows the significance of the contribution.

Atari evaluations use relatively small game subsets (15 or 10 games) for computational reasons, which, combined with the many architecture/normalization variants tested, could raise concerns about the statistical robustness of some fine-grained comparisons despite the use of IQM and bootstrapped CIs.

The paper introduces many additional variants and results (Ensemble Shared Features, MellowMax combination, meta-gradient weighting, mixed precision) that, while interesting, are explored only superficially (single or few games/tasks) and mostly relegated to the appendix, diluting the focus of the main contribution.

strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated and practically relevant problem: reducing the memory overhead of target networks while retaining their stabilizing benefits.

Very broad empirical evaluation spanning online discrete control (Atari, CNN and IMPALA backbones), offline discrete control (CQL), continuous control (SAC/SimbaV2 on DMC Hard), a language-model RL task (ILQL/Wordle with GPT-2), and a streaming RL setting -- this breadth is a genuine strength.

Useful mechanistic analysis (gradient cosine similarity to target-based updates, 'target churn', effective rank/srank) that attempts to explain why sharing features narrows the gap, going beyond a pure black-box performance comparison.

Reasonably thorough ablations on target update period T, number of heads K, and network width, plus a pilot study on mixed-precision training and an alternative 'Ensemble Shared Features' variant, showing some robustness of the core idea.
Reproducibility materials (hyperparameter tables, per-game learning curves, code availability statement) are provided in detail.
weaknesses: The core algorithmic novelty is incremental: it is essentially a straightforward combination of (a) a shared-trunk/frozen-head architecture, which is conceptually similar to existing multi-head Q-network designs (e.g., bootstrapped DQN-style heads), and (b) the already-published iterated Q-network idea (Vincent et al., 2025b), applied here mainly by removing the separate target copy and paying for K linear heads instead.

K (number of parallel Bellman updates/heads) is a new, sensitive hyperparameter whose optimal value varies substantially across domains and even across architectures within the same domain (e.g., K=49 helps with IMPALA but hurts with the plain CNN, K=9 works well in Atari but only matches K=1 in DMC). No principled selection rule is given beyond 'increase K until performance degrades,' which undermines the practical resource-efficiency claim, since tuning requires multiple runs.

The method does not reduce training time or FLOPs (explicitly acknowledged in Section 6/Appendix B), so the practical benefit is restricted to peak memory footprint; for many of the motivating use-cases (large models, edge devices) compute cost is often equally or more limiting than memory, weakening the significance of the contribution.

The 'why it works' analysis (cosine similarity, target churn, srank) is purely empirical/post-hoc and offers no theoretical guarantee or convergence analysis, in contrast to related chaining-value-function work (Schmitt et al., 2022) that provides guarantees for the linear case.

Some reported gains (e.g., iS-DQN K=9 outperforming TB-DQN by 6% AUC, or iS-ILQL beating TB-ILQL by 5%) are based on a fairly small number of seeds/games (5 seeds, 10-15 Atari games) and confidence intervals in several figures visibly overlap between iS variants and target-based baselines, so claims of 'closing' or 'surpassing' the gap should be interpreted cautiously.

The meta-gradient weighting experiment (Appendix D.4) is inconclusive -- learned coefficients converge to uniform weights, essentially showing that this added complexity does not improve over the simple static-sum loss, which is presented as a positive finding but largely just validates that the added machinery was unnecessary.

The extremely long appendix (29 pages vs. 10 main pages) suggests the core result required substantial additional experiments and qualifications to be convincing, and the paper's main text alone does not fully establish robustness of the proposed method without heavy reliance on supplementary material.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: the memory overhead of target networks in deep RL, offering a simple, easy-to-implement solution (sharing all but the last linear layer between online and target networks).

Extremely broad empirical evaluation spanning online and offline discrete control (Atari with CNN and IMPALA architectures), offline conservative Q-learning, continuous control (DMC Hard with SimbaV2/SAC), large-scale language-model-based offline RL (ILQL on Wordle with GPT-2), and streaming RL (Stream Q(λ)) — a genuinely impressive breadth for a single paper.

Method is shown to be orthogonal to and compatible with existing regularization techniques (LayerNorm, BatchNorm, MellowMax), and the paper demonstrates this compatibility empirically rather than just claiming it.
Careful ablations on target update period, number of parallel Bellman updates K, and network width, plus a promising extension using meta-gradients to automatically weight the Bellman-update losses.

Section 5.6 provides genuine mechanistic insight into why the method works (gradient cosine similarity to target-based updates, a novel 'target churn' metric, and effective rank/srank analysis of representation richness), going beyond a purely black-box performance comparison.
Good reproducibility practices: detailed hyperparameter tables, individual per-game learning curves in the appendix, reported FLOPs/training time, and a reproducibility statement.

The generalization to 'Ensemble Shared Features' (Section 5.2) suggests the underlying idea of parameter sharing via linear heads is not limited to iterated Q-learning, strengthening the conceptual contribution.
weaknesses: The core algorithmic novelty is somewhat incremental: it combines two existing ideas (a linear-head target network and iterated Q-learning from Vincent et al. 2025b) rather than introducing a fundamentally new mechanism.

The method introduces a new hyperparameter K whose optimal value is problem- and architecture-dependent (e.g., K=49 helps with IMPALA but hurts with CNN), and while the paper offers a heuristic ('increase K until performance decreases'), this adds tuning burden not present in vanilla target-free or target-based baselines.

As explicitly acknowledged by the authors, iS-QN does not reduce training time or FLOPs compared to target-based methods (except in a special case for ILQL) — the benefit is restricted to memory footprint, which somewhat limits the practical significance relative to the compute-bound nature of many real RL applications.

In several settings (e.g., iS-SAC with K=9 in DMC, ILQL's overall margins), gains over target-free or parity with target-based are modest and confidence intervals often overlap, making some claims of 'closing the gap' or 'outperforming' less than fully convincing.

Atari evaluations use a relatively small subset of games (15 for CNN, 10 for IMPALA) rather than the full benchmark, and only 5 seeds per game, which, while standard for compute-constrained studies, limits statistical power for close comparisons.

The paper does not compare against alternative memory-reduction strategies mentioned in the related work (e.g., pruning, sparse training, quantization) as empirical baselines, only combining with mixed-precision training in a brief pilot study.

The mechanistic explanations (gradient similarity, target churn, srank) are informative but largely correlational/post-hoc rather than derived from a theoretical analysis of why sharing features specifically improves stability.
